ubo_and_aml_profiling.pep_and_sanctions_screening_protocols: Mandatory risk-based screening against the PEP definition in s 5 of the AML/CFT Act 2009 (domestic, foreign and international-organization PEPs), the United Nations Security Council consolidated sanctions list implemented under the United Nations Sanctions Act 1981, the New Zealand targeted sanctions list administered by the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and Trade, the OFAC Specially Designated Nationals and Blocked Persons List (required because the target payment rails are Swift Wire and Standby LC in USD/foreign currency), the UK Sanctions List and the EU consolidated list. For ISIC 5222 offshore marine fuel bunkering, the onboarding bank, as a reporting entity supervised by the Reserve Bank of New Zealand, will require enhanced customer due diligence, including name matching under the AML/CFT (Name Matching) Regulations 2011, source-of-funds verification, vessel-level AIS position checks to counter trade-based money laundering, and 90-day post-incorporation transaction monitoring. The AML risk tier is Medium_Risk_Enhanced.

statutory_name_clearance_protocol.registry_portal_name: New Zealand Companies Office - 'Reserve a Name / Register a Company' online service at companies-register.companiesoffice.govt.nz, integrated with the New Zealand Business Number (NZBN) portal
statutory_name_clearance_protocol.language_and_transliteration_doctrine: A New Zealand company legal name must use the Latin (Roman) alphabet; names may be in English or te reo Maori. Non-Latin scripts such as Chinese characters, Cyrillic or Arabic script are not registerable as the legal name; a transliteration into Latin script (for example pinyin for Chinese-origin trade names) is required and must be recorded as the registered legal name. The name must end with 'Limited' or the permitted abbreviation 'Ltd' unless an exemption applies under s 21 of the Companies Act 1993. Allowed characters include letters, numerals 0-9, hyphens, apostrophes, ampersands, parentheses and spaces; otherwise the name must consist of logical Roman-alphabet transliteration and must not be identical or almost identical to an existing reserved, registered or protected name under ss 24-25 of the Act.

statutory_name_clearance_protocol.extension_and_rejection_appeal_sop: A name reservation is valid for 20 working days from the date of the Registrar's approval and cannot be statutorily extended; if the reservation lapses, the applicant may immediately lodge a fresh reservation application. Upon a notice of refusal, the applicant or its New Zealand incorporation agent may, within 20 working days, file a written reconsideration request with the New Zealand Companies Office under s 26 of the Companies Act 1993, attaching evidence of acquired goodwill, visual or phonetic distinction from the conflicting name, or any requisite ministerial consent under s 23. If the Registrar confirms the refusal, the applicant may appeal to the High Court of New Zealand pursuant to s 26 of the Companies Act 1993, or in the alternative seek judicial review; at all stages the holder of the conflicting name may be requested to provide a written s 25 consent to registration of the similar name, which if obtained converts the application to an allowable one.

registered_office_and_commercial_substan.virtual_office_permissibility: Permissible only in a constrained form. The registered office must be a genuine physical street address in New Zealand where the company's records and the ultimate shareholder register are kept, satisfying s 178 of the Companies Act 1993; a PO Box or poste-restante address alone is statutorily invalid. A serviced-office or licensed virtual-office product providing a physical New Zealand suite, mail handling, document scanning and authorized receipt of legal service is acceptable. For the ISIC 5222 marine bunkering industry, the Department of Internal Affairs and Inland Revenue will expect a documented commercial-substance narrative comprising the physical operations location or charter arrangements, bunker supply contracts, insurance coverage, bank account, and a decision-making location in New Zealand rather than a pure mail-drop arrangement.
registered_office_and_commercial_substan.physical_inspection_likelihood: Moderate quantified risk: approximately 20-35% annual probability of an unannounced on-site compliance inspection by the Department of Internal Affairs (AML/CFT supervision) or a premises verification by the Inland Revenue Department; the probability increases to above 50% where a beneficial owner is a foreign PEP or where bunkering records, vessel position logs or source-of-funds evidence are incomplete. The use of a serviced office does not reduce this inspection risk.

incorporation_legal_framework.governing_statute_and_sections: Companies Act 1993 (NZ), Part 2 (ss. 10–18: incorporation, legal capacity and certificate of incorporation), ss. 20–25 (company names), ss. 27–33 (constitution and adoption), ss. 87–94 (no-par-value shares and allotment/issue of shares), ss. 122–131 (board powers), ss. 147–151 (director residency requirements), ss. 200–201 (statutory records), ss. 213–216 (registered office and address for service); supplemented by the Companies (Fees) Regulations 2011 (incorporation fee NZD 150) and the Financial Reporting Act 2013.
incorporation_legal_framework.competent_registry_authority: Registrar of Companies — New Zealand Companies Office, a business unit of the Ministry of Business, Innovation and Employment (MBIE); online statutory portal: Companies Register (companies-register.companiesoffice.govt.nz), authenticated via RealMe.
incorporation_legal_framework.statutory_filing_instrument: Online Application for Incorporation under s. 12 of the Companies Act 1993, executed through the Companies Register 'Incorporate a Company' service, with the resulting Certificate of Incorporation and automatic issuance of the New Zealand Business Number (NZBN) under the New Zealand Business Number Act 2016.
incorporation_legal_framework.minimum_paid_up_capital_rule: No statutory minimum paid-up capital: shares may be issued for any consideration, including a nil or deferred subscription price, and need not be fully paid (Companies Act 1993, s. 94). There is no capital escrow account, banker's guarantee or paid-up-capital deposit certificate required for incorporation. Any subscriber funds if contributed remain at the free disposition of the company.

national_tax_registration_infrastructure.competent_tax_authority: Inland Revenue Department (Te Tari Tauhokohoko, IRD) — the sole competent national tax authority; all registrations, returns, and payments are administered through the myIR secure online portal (https://www.ird.govt.nz). Export clearance and customs control are administered separately by the New Zealand Customs Service (Ngā Kaitiaki o Te Ritepu).
national_tax_registration_infrastructure.tax_id_procurement_sop: For the non-resident International Company (CK_IC): (1) Determine NZ taxable presence — a Cook Islands International Company incorporated under the International Companies Act operating as an exempt offshore entity and not carrying on a taxable activity in New Zealand is outside the NZ income tax net and requires no NZ IRD number for income tax. (2) If the entity establishes a fixed establishment, branch, or performs taxable marine bunkering activity in New Zealand, apply for an IRD number by submitting Form IR742 (Company IRD Number Application) accompanied by certificate of incorporation, constitutional documents, and director/beneficial ownership particulars. (3) Register for GST through myIR (or Form IR322 for non-resident applicants) when actual or expected taxable supplies exceed NZD 60,000 in any 12-month period; voluntary GST registration is available and is commercially recommended for a bunkering supplier seeking to zero-rate international ship stores and recover input tax. (4) Activate myIR customer access, obtain the GST registration number, and appoint a New Zealand bank account or foreign-currency settlement facility for GST refunds and IRD correspondence. (5) File all GST returns electronically in accordance with the assigned filing frequency (monthly, two-monthly, or six-monthly) and maintain seven-year record retention for export substantiation.
national_tax_registration_infrastructure.default_entity_tax_classification: Tax_Exempt_Zone — A Cook Islands-style International Company (CK_IC) that is non-resident, holds no New Zealand fixed establishment, and derives no New Zealand-sourced income is exempt from New Zealand income tax and may hold a limited-scope GST registration solely for zero-rated international marine bunkering supplies. By contrast, a New Zealand-resident company or a foreign company with a New Zealand permanent establishment is subject to Entity_Level_Taxation at the 28% corporate rate unless a Look-Through Company election is made.
national_tax_registration_infrastructure.statutory_election_mechanisms: New Zealand does not operate a US-style check-the-box regime; entity classification is determined by domestic tax law. Available statutory elections: (1) Look-Through Company (LTC) election under Form IR427 for close-held companies, conferring Pass_Through_Eligible treatment; (2) consolidated group and imputation group elections under the Income Tax Act 2007; (3) GST group registration and GST branch registration under sections 55 and 54 of the Goods and Services Tax Act 1985; (4) hybrid and branch mismatch defensive elections and adjustments under Subpart FH and section GB 52 of the Income Tax Act 2007 aligned with OECD BEPS Action 2; (5) optional zero-rating elections and secondhand goods elections relevant to marine stores and vessel supplies.

indirect_taxation_nexus_and_rules.indirect_tax_system_name: GST (Goods and Services Tax) — a value-added consumption tax legislated under the Goods and Services Tax Act 1985 and administered by the Inland Revenue Department
indirect_taxation_nexus_and_rules.statutory_registration_threshold_local_c: NZD 60,000 of actual or expected taxable supplies in any 12-month period (sections 51 and 52, GST Act 1985). A non-resident supplier of remote services or low-value imported goods to New Zealand consumers must register when supplies to NZ exceed NZD 60,000 per annum. Voluntary registration is available for marine bunkering suppliers to support zero-rated export supplies and input tax recovery.
indirect_taxation_nexus_and_rules.electronic_invoicing_and_clearance_manda: No mandatory e-invoicing, real-time fiscal clearance, or digital stamping regime exists in New Zealand. E-invoicing is voluntary and operates interoperably through the Peppol network administered by the NZ Peppol Authority. GST obligations are discharged via electronic returns in myIR without API-based invoice pre-clearance by Inland Revenue. Suppliers must nonetheless issue and retain GST invoices, including electronic format, recording recipient details, consideration, GST-exclusive value, and the statutory zero-rating basis for marine bunker supplies; the retained export evidence package operates as the functional substitute for fiscal clearance.

export_zero_rating_and_refund_substantia.zero_rating_eligibility: Zero-rating is available under section 11(1)(m) of the GST Act 1985 for supplies of bunker fuel, lubricants, and ship stores delivered to the master or owner of a craft that is or will be engaged in international (non-New Zealand coastal) travel for reward, provided the goods are solely for use as stores during international travel; related port, towage, mooring, and maintenance services supplied to international craft are zero-rated under section 11A(2)(b). General export zero-rating under section 11(1)(a) applies where the supplier exports the goods from New Zealand, with Inland Revenue practice requiring physical export and documented shipment within 28 days of the time of supply. The supplier must hold contemporaneous evidence of export and of the vessel's international voyage itinerary; supplies to coastally-trading, fishing, or non-international vessels remain standard-rated at 15%.
mandatory_customs_documentation_bundle: Customs export declaration lodged with the New Zealand Customs Service (Integrated Cargo System export entry with approved exit status)
Bill of Lading or Sea Waybill evidencing discharge at an international port outside New Zealand
Bunker Delivery Note (BDN) signed by the master detailing quantity, grade, IMO number, and port of delivery
Vessel certificate of registry or IMO tonnage certificate evidencing the craft's international voyage status
Inward foreign currency remittance certificate and SWIFT MT103 wire confirmation evidencing receipt of export consideration from the charterer or shipowner
Voyage log or port itinerary demonstrating a foreign destination and confirming the craft is not engaged in New Zealand coastal trade
export_zero_rating_and_refund_substantia.audit_scrutiny_and_clawback_penalties: Inland Revenue may, upon audit, disregard export evidence and claw back the zero-rating, assessing GST at 15% on the full supply consideration plus use-of-money interest from the original due date under Parts 7 and 12 of the Tax Administration Act 1994. Shortfall penalties under section 141 scale from 20% (failure to take reasonable care or unacceptable tax position) to 40% (gross carelessness), 100% (abusive tax position), and 150% (evasion). Deliberate fraudulent bunkering zero-rating claims expose the International Company and its officers to criminal prosecution under sections 143A and 143B of the Tax Administration Act 1994, carrying fines of up to NZD 50,000 per offence and, for individuals, imprisonment of up to five years; director and promoter liability may be imposed under section 149. Given the Medium_Risk_Enhanced AML tier applicable to ISIC_5222 marine bunkering, IRD and NZ Customs jointly scrutinize BDN-to-remittance matching, vessel AIS data, and same-vessel resupply patterns, and all substantiation records must be retained for seven years.

fx_control_regime_and_central_bank_regul.central_bank_authority: Reserve Bank of New Zealand (RBNZ) in conjunction with the Financial Markets Authority (FMA) under the Anti-Money Laundering and Countering Financing of Terrorism Act 2009; New Zealand maintains no separate foreign exchange control authority due to the freely floating New Zealand dollar (NZD).
fx_control_regime_and_central_bank_regul.currency_convertibility_assessment: New Zealand operates a fully liberalised and open capital and current account regime. The NZD is freely convertible for trade, investment, and profit remittance. There are no restrictions on capital account transactions, no inward/outward capital approval requirements, and no exchange controls applicable to non-resident entities. Profit remittances, dividends, and repatriations are not subject to exchange control approval; however, obtaining bank financing or maintaining a corporate account may be subject to AML/FATCA/CRS compliance and non-resident withholding tax (NRWT) or approved issuer levy (AIL) obligations on dividends, while no withholding tax applies to principal repayment or capital gains in the ordinary course.
fx_control_regime_and_central_bank_regul.export_proceeds_surrender_rules: There are no statutory export proceeds surrender rules, mandatory conversion ratios, or repatriation timelines in New Zealand. Exporters are free to hold foreign currency proceeds in offshore or onshore accounts; however, for statistical and AML reporting, funds credited to a New Zealand bank account must be accompanied by a valid transaction narrative and, where applicable, the New Zealand Customs Service export entry and underlying commercial documentation.

corporate_banking_onboarding_blueprint.fintech_emi_cross_border_viability: Low to Medium. Offshore digital EMI providers without a New Zealand registered branch cannot open a domestic settlement account in NZD for corporate use. Non-bank money service providers may be used for limited inbound/outbound USD or EUR transactions, but they face heightened AML/KYC and licensing constraints under the Financial Service Providers (Registration and Disputes Resolution) Act 2008 and are not a substitute for a full RBNZ-regulated current account for bunkering trade settlement or standby letters of credit.
corporate_banking_onboarding_blueprint.physical_presence_and_kyc_interview_mand: Physical presence of all directors is no longer universally mandatory; major New Zealand banks permit remote onboarding via interactive video (KYC interview) for non-resident directors, subject to certification of passport identity, proof of residential address, and independent verification of corporate existence and beneficial ownership. In practice, a physical meeting is still preferred where an International Company is non-resident, has no local economic footprint, and engages in high-volume marine bunkering trade; a physically present New Zealand-based director or a director with a verifiable professional address materially improves approval speed.

critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.trigger_point: Non-resident International Company with no local New Zealand physical presence or material economic nexus
critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.evidentiary_defense_dossier: Certified company certificate of incorporation, constitution, register of directors/ultimate beneficial owners (UBO), a New Zealand registered office or CPA/reference address, an economic substance memorandum demonstrating actual bunkering contracts, charter party agreements, vessel evidence, supplier invoices, and client-side due diligence records.

critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.trigger_point: UBO or director tax residence in a high-risk or FATF-grey-listed jurisdiction
critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.evidentiary_defense_dossier: Tax residency certificates, official government-issued photo ID, source of wealth/income documentation (audited financial statements, trust deed, asset valuation), employment or business ownership history, and a written source-of-funds declaration for all inbound capital injections.

critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.trigger_point: Bunkering industry flagged as medium-risk enhanced due to potential marine fuel smuggling, sanctions, or false export declarations
critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.evidentiary_defense_dossier: Valid maritime fuel supplier licence (where applicable), ISO 9001/ISO 14001 certifications, ISM/ISPS compliance certificates, vessel registration and flagged vessel list, final customer KYC file (ship owner/operator), bill of lading, customs declarations, HS code descriptions, and signed anti-money-laundering undertaking confirming the company will not accept cash payments above statutory thresholds.

critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.trigger_point: Cross-border wire transactions to or from counterparties without prior banking relationship
critical_aml_kyc_blockers_and_defense.evidentiary_defense_dossier: Duly executed bunkering sales contract and credit policy, shipping schedules, proforma invoices, verified counterparty independent company registry excerpt, and confirmatory evidence that the underlying commodity is physical bunker fuel rather than a financial marker.

cross_border_liquidity_and_clearing_rail.inbound_capital_injection_routing: Inbound equity or shareholder loan capital must be transferred via SWIFT MT103 with the exact beneficiary legal name, the International Company's account number and bank identity, and a purpose narrative 'Inward Foreign Direct Investment – Ordinary Share Capital/Shareholder Loan' (or equivalent commercial purpose description). For New Zealand statistical reporting, the bank will assign a standard economic activity code; the funds should be accompanied by a board resolution authorising the capital injection, a share subscription agreement, a shareholder loan agreement, and proof of source of funds. No NZD conversion restrictions apply; if transferred in foreign currency, the receiving New Zealand bank will either deposit into a multi-currency account or convert at free-market rate without mandatory quotation approval. For amounts above NZD 10,000 equivalent, AML checks apply and counterparty bank must be SWIFT-compliant.
cross_border_liquidity_and_clearing_rail.outbound_trade_disbursements: Outbound bunkering and lubricant supply payments are cleared via the Society for Worldwide Interbank Financial Telecommunication (SWIFT) network as MT103 customer credit transfers for operating expenses and inventory; settlement of high-value New Zealand-dollar payments should use the RBNZ Exchange Settlement Account System (ESAS) operated by the New Zealand Clearing and Settlement System. For credit-supported bunkering sales, downstream charterers or buyers may require a Standby Letter of Credit (SBLC) or documentary Irrevocable Commercial Letter of Credit, issued by a prime international bank and advised through a New Zealand bank, payable on presentation of delivery receipts, BDN, quantity surveyor certificate, and compliant invoice. Bulk fuel payments to major trading counterparties are customarily routed by SWIFT MT103 with an explicit 'Invoice No., Vessel Name, Port, Bunkering Date' narrative to assist reconciliation and sanctions screening.
permissible_fx_hedging_instruments: Non-deliverable forwards (NDFs) rarely required because NZD is fully convertible but available via major desks when USD liquidity is constrained
Cross-currency basis swap (XCCY swap) for USD/NZD or EUR/NZD principal and interest exchange
FX swap (swap against forward, rollover of maturing contracts)
Market-standard FX options (plain vanilla call/put) and zero-cost collars for fuel price and currency exposure

annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.statutory_deliverable: Annual Return - Companies Act 1993, Part 10, Sections 115-142
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.receiving_authority: New Zealand Companies Office, Registrar of Companies, Ministry of Business, Innovation and Employment
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.statutory_deadline_window: Due within 13 months of incorporation, and thereafter at intervals not exceeding 13 months; the return date is the anniversary of registration, with a Registrar reminder issued approximately 28 days before the due date
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.delinquency_sanctions: Late filing constitutes an offence under s 142 Companies Act 1993, with a fine up to NZD 10,000 for the company and each director; continued non-filing triggers a 20-working-day strike-off notice under s 318 and administrative removal from the New Zealand Companies Register

annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.statutory_deliverable: Financial Statements and Statutory Audit Opinion - Companies Act 1993, Sections 196-202; Financial Reporting Act 2013
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.receiving_authority: New Zealand Companies Office (only for FMC reporting entities and where filing is mandatory); audit report issued by an independent New Zealand-licensed auditor
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.statutory_deadline_window: Financial statements and audit must be completed within 5 months after balance date; where filing with the Companies Office is required, the signed financial statements must be lodged within 20 working days after adoption
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.delinquency_sanctions: Failure to prepare, audit, or file financial statements when required is an offence under the Financial Reporting Act 2013 (fine up to NZD 30,000 per breach); directors also face fines under the Companies Act 1993, and the Registrar may issue a compliance notice or strike off the company for continued default

annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.statutory_deliverable: Annual Statutory Register Audit and On-Site Records Set - Socio-Economic: Registers of Members, Directors, Directors' Interests, and Minute Book
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.receiving_authority: Maintained at the registered office; produced to the New Zealand Companies Office or Registrar of Companies on demand
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.statutory_deadline_window: Review and update concurrently with the preparation of each annual return; registers must be complete and accurate at all times and available for inspection during business hours
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.delinquency_sanctions: Failure to maintain required registers and records is an offence under ss 201-202 Companies Act 1993, with a fine up to NZD 10,000; the Registrar may compel the production of records and seek compliance orders

annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.statutory_deliverable: AML/CFT Compliance Programme Annual Risk Refresh and Independent Assurance Review - if the entity is an AML/CFT reporting entity
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.receiving_authority: Independent AML/CFT assurance provider; report retained and produced to the AML/CFT supervisor (Reserve Bank of New Zealand or Department of Internal Affairs) on demand
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.statutory_deadline_window: Independent review at least every two years under s 60 Anti-Money Laundering and Countering Financing of Terrorism Act 2009; risk assessment and compliance programme updated on an annual rolling basis and whenever the bunkering supply model or customer profile changes
annual_compliance_calendar_matrix.delinquency_sanctions: Non-compliance invites civil liability orders up to NZD 2,000,000 for a body corporate and NZD 200,000 for an individual, plus monetary penalties and potential restrictions on licensed business operations

statutory_audit_and_accounting_mandate.compulsory_audit_thresholds: Mandatory independent audit applies to FMC reporting entities; large companies; and companies where shareholders holding at least 5% of voting rights request an audit under s 199 Companies Act 1993. A company is large if it exceeds at least two of: total assets NZD 60 million, total revenue NZD 30 million, or 50 or more employees. The Registrar may also direct an audit under s 200 Companies Act 1993.
statutory_audit_and_accounting_mandate.governing_accounting_framework: Financial Reporting Act 2013; New Zealand equivalents to IFRS (NZ IFRS) and the NZ IFRS Reduced Disclosure Regime (NZ IFRS RDR), as issued by the External Reporting Board (XRB)

corporate_registers_and_ubo_annual_confi.ubo_annual_confirmation_protocol: New Zealand does not maintain a separate annual UBO certificate filing. The annual return must confirm current directors and the share register as at the return date. Share transfers are recorded promptly in the Register of Members under s 90 Companies Act 1993, and the Companies Office database is updated on the next annual return or via interim transaction filings. Beneficial ownership records, where relevant to AML/CFT obligations, must be retained for 5 years and disclosed to the supervisor on request.
mandatory_on_site_statutory_registers: Register of Directors' Interests (s 87 Companies Act 1993)
Minute Book of directors' and shareholders' meetings (s 190 Companies Act 1993)

recurring_annual_maintenance_budget_usd.registered_office_or_agent_market_range_: USD 650-1,500 per year (market range for New Zealand registered office address plus professional corporate secretarial maintenance)
recurring_annual_maintenance_budget_usd.statutory_audit_estimated_fee_usd: USD 4,000-12,000 per year (typical private company audit fee for a marine bunkering supply entity; subject to transaction volume and group complexity)

corporate_income_tax_regime.effective_tax_rate_incentives: New Zealand applies a flat corporate income tax rate of 28% with no general tax holiday regime. Specific incentives relevant to marine fuel supply activities are limited. The main effective-rate levers include: (i) the ability to claim deductible expenditure for bunker fuel procurement, freight, vessel operating costs, and charter hire under ordinary business expense rules; (ii) the Research and Development Tax Incentive providing a 15% tax credit on eligible R&D expenditure, generally not applicable to routine bunkering logistics; (iii) the Approved Issuer Levy regime reducing the withholding tax on interest paid to non-residents on certain cross-border debt from the statutory 15% to 2%, where the issuer is an approved issuer; and (iv) imputation credit rules (New Zealand imputation credits) which attach to dividends paid to New Zealand-resident shareholders, preventing economic double taxation at the shareholder level. For a Cook Islands International Company operating through a New Zealand fixed establishment or carrying on a taxable activity in New Zealand, New Zealand-source income derived from ship bunkering and refueling services in territorial waters would be subject to the 28% rate without concessional industry-specific deductions beyond standard depletion of depreciable fuel storage infrastructure.

tax_return_filing_anatomy.form_identifier_and_portal: IR4 (Company Income Tax Return) filed via Inland Revenue's MyIR secure online portal (www.ird.govt.nz). Non-resident companies carrying on business through a fixed establishment in New Zealand also complete the IR4 and accompanying financial statements and tax reconciliation schedules. Where a non-resident company derives New Zealand-source income not attributable to a fixed establishment, IR3 (Non-resident individual/company return) may be relevant for certain withholding obligations, but the corporate return for an IC conducting taxable activity is the IR4.
tax_return_filing_anatomy.statutory_deadline_rule: An IR4 return for a standard 31 March balance date must be filed and the terminal tax paid by 7 April following the end of the income year. Companies not on a 31 March balance date may use a different accounting balance date approved by Inland Revenue, and the filing/payment deadline is the 7th day of the fourth month after the balance date (e.g. 7 July for a 31 March year-end; for a 30 June balance date, 7 October). Where the company has a tax agent with an extension of time arrangement, filing deadlines may be extended to the 7th day of the eighth month after balance date for tax agents with an extension of time to file (generally 7 November for a 31 March balance date), but payment of terminal tax may still be due 7 April unless provisional tax instalments have been correctly managed. Non-resident companies with no New Zealand fixed establishment generally have tax withheld at source and are not required to file an IR4 unless claiming a refund or carrying on a taxable activity.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Business income or loss: total New Zealand-sourced gross income, including bunkering service revenue, supply of marine fuel, lubricant replenishment fees, and incidental wharfage or logistics charges, before deduction of expenses.
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: Enter all income derived from New Zealand sources, including income from the sale or delivery of bunker fuel to vessels within New Zealand territorial waters or from a fixed fuel storage facility in New Zealand. Do not include foreign-source income unless the company is an IC treated as resident in New Zealand under tie-breaker rules.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Total income: aggregates business income with any interest, dividends, and other assessable income. A foreign-owned non-resident company must separately disclose non-resident withholding tax (NRWT) deducted on any New Zealand-sourced interest and dividends.
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: Include any New Zealand-sourced interest on deposits or loans secured against New Zealand assets and any dividends paid by a New Zealand company to the non-resident IC. Items subject to NRWT must be disclosed even if the tax has already been final withholding.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Business expenses: deductible expenditure incurred in deriving assessable income, including purchases of bunker fuel, port dues, crew costs if on New Zealand payroll, maintenance of storage tanks, transport and logistics, and depreciation on fuel storage and dispensing infrastructure.
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: Expenses must be apportioned on a reasonable basis where the IC earns both New Zealand and foreign-source income. Only deduct expenses incurred in deriving New Zealand assessable income. Transactions with related foreign entities must satisfy the arm's length standard and be supported by contemporaneous transfer pricing documentation.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Net profit or loss before taxes: gross income minus all apportioned deductible expenses, reflecting the accounting result adjusted for tax timing differences (e.g. depreciation adjustments, prepayments, provisions).
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: For a Cook Islands IC operating in New Zealand, the net taxable income attributable to the New Zealand permanent establishment or fixed establishment must be computed as the profit the IC would have derived if it were a distinct and separate enterprise performing the same or similar activities under the same or similar conditions.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Non-resident withholding tax paid on interest/dividends: claims a credit for NRWT already deducted at source on New Zealand-sourced interest or dividends received by the IC.
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: Only claim credits where the payer deducted NRWT and paid it to Inland Revenue. The IC must attach a statement showing the gross amount, the NRWT rate applied, and the tax withheld.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Trans-Tasman imputation credit and dividend information: reports franked or imputed dividends received from Australian resident companies and identifies the IC's shareholding relationship for anti-avoidance analysis.
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: Complete only where the IC receives dividends from an Australian company that carries imputation credits. A non-resident IC may be entitled to a refundable credit under the Trans-Tasman imputation rules in limited circumstances if the dividend is from a New Zealand/Australian dual-listed company.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Loss offset: current-year or prior-year net losses applied against assessable income, with the residual loss carried forward.
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: A non-resident IC carrying on business in New Zealand may carry forward losses only if the company satisfies the continuity of ownership or same business rules. For the 5-year loss carryforward limit observed under this jurisdiction's tax classification, attach a loss continuity schedule and be aware that ownership continuity of greater than 49% must be maintained unless the same or similar business test applies.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Related-party cross-border transaction disclosure: transactions with overseas related parties exceeding NZD 1 million in aggregate for goods or services, or NZD 500,000 for interest-free or otherwise non-arm's length financing, must be reported in the IR4 International Dealings Schedule (IR4S).
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: Disclose all payments to or from the Cook Islands parent or sister entities for bunker fuel procurement, charter hire, management fees, royalties, and financing. Attach the IR4S along with a transfer pricing position statement confirming the application of the OECD Transfer Pricing Guidelines.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Imputation credit account (ICA) balance: for companies resident in New Zealand, the closing imputation credit account balance and dividends credited during the year. A Cook Islands IC is generally not resident in New Zealand unless management and control is exercised in New Zealand; therefore this box may be nil.
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: If the IC is managed and controlled in New Zealand and therefore becomes tax-resident, maintain the ICA and attach a copy of the dividend resolution. If the IC is not New Zealand-resident, leave nil and ensure no New Zealand-resident shareholder personally controls the company to avoid deemed residency.

field_by_field_filling_dissection.entry_description: Attribution of profits of the foreign company: records whether New Zealand has taxed the IC on a look-through basis and identifies any CFC or FIF adjustments attributable to a New Zealand-resident shareholder.
field_by_field_filling_dissection.non_resident_entry_guidance: Nil for a genuine non-resident IC unless a New Zealand resident holds more than 10% of the shares and the IC is a controlled foreign company. Fatal red flag: a New Zealand-resident de facto shareholder with management control can trigger CFC attribution and full New Zealand taxation of worldwide income.

tax_return_filing_anatomy.failure_penalties: Late filing penalties are imposed under the Tax Administration Act 1994. A non-resident company failing to file an IR4 by the due date is liable to a late filing penalty of NZD 250 for the first day and NZD 250 per month (or part-month) thereafter, up to a maximum of NZD 2,000 for a company. In addition, late payment of tax attracts an initial late payment penalty of 1% of the unpaid amount immediately upon default, a further 1% late payment penalty imposed at the end of the 7th day, again at the end of the 14th day, and then 1.5% per month for the remaining period until the tax is paid. Inland Revenue may also charge use-of-money interest on unpaid terminal tax at a prescribed rate (currently approximately 9.02% per annum for underpayments as of the current rate-setting cycle, adjusted quarterly). Where the failure to file is intentional or reckless, a stricter penalty of up to 150% of the tax shortfall may be imposed under the civil penalty regime, and a person who aids or abets evasion is liable to imprisonment under criminal revenue statutes.

profit_repatriation_and_withholding_tax.statutory_dividend_wht_rate: 15% for non-resident companies receiving dividends from a New Zealand resident company. Where the dividend is fully imputed and the shareholder is a New Zealand-resident company, no NRWT applies; for non-residents, imputation credits do not reduce NRWT except under certain fully imputed dividend elections. The independent family company election and transitional resident rules do not apply here. For a Cook Islands IC, the statutory NRWT rate on outgoing dividends paid by a New Zealand subsidiary to the IC is 15%. If the dividend is paid by the IC itself as a New Zealand-resident company to its Cook Islands shareholder, the same 15% NRWT applies.
profit_repatriation_and_withholding_tax.treaty_relief_application_protocol: New Zealand's Double Tax Agreement with the Cook Islands: The New Zealand-Cook Islands DTA applies. Dividend withholding tax under the DTA is 15% generally, with a reduced rate of 5% if the beneficial owner is a company that holds directly at least 10% of the voting power of the paying company (provided the company is not entitled to a special tax regime in the Cook Islands, and subject to limitation of benefits provisions). To invoke treaty relief, the non-resident IC must (i) obtain a Certificate of Residence from the Cook Islands Ministry of Finance and Economic Management, which must be in the form required by the competent authority and show the IC is fiscally resident in the Cook Islands; (ii) deliver the certificate to the New Zealand paying company before or within the time prescribed in the NRWT rules, generally before payment; (iii) provide a declaration of beneficial ownership and, where applicable, evidence of the 10% shareholding (e5). The withholding agent applies the reduced rate based on the certificate; where no certificate is provided, the statutory 15% rate or 30% further withholding for non-declared payees may apply under the NRWT rules (non-resident withholding tax on interest and dividends is 15%; for non-resident companies not filing declarations the payer must operate 30% withholding if the recipient is non-resident and no declaration is held). Taxpayers may also file for a refund of over-withheld tax through an IR3 or IR4 return. The protocol requires that the Cook Islands IC notify the New Zealand competent authority if its entitlement to benefits ceases.
profit_repatriation_and_withholding_tax.cross_border_royalty_and_interest_wht: Statutory interest withholding tax (NRWT) on interest paid by a New Zealand company to a non-resident is 15%. Under the New Zealand-Cook Islands DTA, the interest withholding tax rate is 10% where the beneficial owner is a resident of the Cook Islands. Where the interest is paid to an approved issuer and the borrower is an approved issuer, the Approved Issuer Levy (AIL) regime reduces the effective withholding cost to 2%, payable by the borrower, and is an alternative to NRWT for qualifying debentures and registered securities publicly offered; however, for related-party intercompany loans not publicly offered, AIL generally does not apply and NRWT at 10% under the DTA applies. Statutory royalty withholding tax is 15% under domestic law; under the NZ-Cook Islands DTA, royalties are generally taxed in the source country at 10% of the gross amount (the DTA's royalty rate is 10%). Where the royalty arises in New Zealand but is paid to a Cook Islands IC that is the beneficial owner, the reduced 10% DTA rate applies provided residence certification is furnished. No withholding tax is imposed on the payment of dividends or interest by a New Zealand branch of a non-resident company to its head office in respect of internal funding as those are equity/notional items, but branch profit attribution rules apply and a branch repatriation remittance tax does not exist separately; however, the approved enterprise or branch returns must attribute a level of taxable capital to the New Zealand branch under the thin capitalisation rules.

transfer_pricing_and_economic_substance.tp_documentation_threshold_local_currenc: Inland Revenue requires mandatory disclosure of cross-border related-party transactions on the IR4S where total transactions between the New Zealand business and overseas related parties exceed NZD 1 million in aggregate per income year, or where financing arrangements with overseas related parties exceed NZD 500,000 (including short-term trade credit) and are not at arm's length. Full transfer pricing documentation (Local File) must be prepared where the aggregate value of cross-border related-party transactions is NZD 1 million or more for goods/services, NZD 1 million for intangibles, and NZD 1 million for financing transactions specifically under New Zealand's Schedule 20 disclosure requirements. Important: New Zealand does not have statutory Local File/Master File thresholds identical to OECD Action 13 of NZD 1 million in all cases; the documentation obligations are driven by the IR4S disclosure schedule and the requirement to maintain contemporaneous documentation sufficient to show arm's length outcomes for all cross-border related-party arrangements. The New Zealand Master File obligation effectively applies to significant enterprises with revenue over NZD 100 million and related-party transactions over NZD 10 million in aggregate; an IC acting as a conduit for fuel procurement from the Cook Islands parent would be required to prepare and, if requested, submit a Master File within 30 days of the Information Request. In all cases, documentation must be prepared before the tax return filing date to be contemporaneous.
approved_arm_length_methodologies: CUP, Resale Price, Cost Plus, TNMM, Profit Split
transfer_pricing_and_economic_substance.economic_substance_doctrine: New Zealand applies a general anti-avoidance rule (GAAR) under section BG 1 of the Income Tax Act 2007, which voids tax avoidance arrangements; a Cook Islands IC operating a bunkering business in New Zealand must demonstrate real commercial substance, including operational decision-making, physical fuel storage or logistics activity, local risk management, and the presence of employees or agents in New Zealand. Although New Zealand does not apply the OECD-style Economic Substance Regulations (ESR) of the Caribbean or UAE, the thin capitalisation rules (75% debt-to-asset safe harbour for non-resident-owned companies) and the related-party financing rules impose substance-based limitations. A shell company without local substance may be disregarded as a sham, and the GAAR may reconstruct the IC's financing, royalty, and service fee arrangements. The IC must be able to evidence: (i) a New Zealand bank account, (ii) local operational contracts, (iii) independent directors if structured as a Cook Islands entity, (iv) actual meetings held outside New Zealand, and (v) arm's length remuneration for any New Zealand agent. The 'economic substance doctrine' in the context of the New Zealand-Cook Islands DTA also arises through the limitation of benefits clause requiring the IC to be a bona fide resident with real continuous presence, not a conduit.

fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.infraction_category: Tax Evasion via Understatement of Bunkering Revenue
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.triggering_act: Deliberately omitting cash sales of marine fuel, false invoicing of vessel supplies, or failing to declare income derived from bunkering services provided to foreign vessels within New Zealand territorial waters.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.statutory_sanction: Under section 143A of the Tax Administration Act 1994, evasion of tax is a criminal offence punishable on conviction by imprisonment for a term not exceeding five years and a fine of up to NZD 50,000 for the first offence, plus a fine of up to NZD 50,000 in respect of each subsequent offence. Civil shortfall penalties under section 141I can be up to 150% of the tax shortfall for evasion or an abusive tax position. Inland Revenue can also impose late payment penalties and use-of-money interest on the entire evaded base.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.personal_liability_of_directors: Directors who knowingly sign false tax returns, direct the concealment of sales, or benefit from the evasion may be prosecuted personally. Under section 149 of the Tax Administration Act, directors are jointly and severally liable with the company for tax liabilities incurred through the company's default where the default is attributable to the director's act or omission and the director failed to take reasonable steps to prevent it. Criminal conviction may bring imprisonment up to 5 years, travel bans under the Criminal Proceeds Recovery Act 2009, and confiscation of personal and corporate assets. Civil restitution includes full repayment of evaded tax, shortfall penalties of up to 150%, and disqualification from managing a company under the Companies Act 1993.

fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.triggering_act: The Cook Islands IC holds a New Zealand bunkering contract, receives revenue, pays management fees to a related entity, and repatriates profits to the Cook Islands while all operational decisions, procurement, invoicing, and banking are controlled from a tax haven with no local staff, premises, or risk-bearing. The arrangement is structured to wash out taxable profit in New Zealand via excessive service fees or non-arm's length charter hire.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.statutory_sanction: The General Anti-Avoidance Rule (BG 1) allows Inland Revenue to reconstruct the arrangement and deny the tax benefit entirely; the IC may be assessed as if no intercompany fees were paid, resulting in tax at 28% on the full gross margin plus non-dissection penalties of up to 100% of the shortfall for taking an unacceptable tax position lacking a reasonable basis. Thin capitalisation recharacterisation may treat excessive debt as equity, disallowing interest deductions and imposing non-resident withholding tax plus approved issuer levy penalties. Repeated abuse may lead to deregistration of the New Zealand branch and denial of the DTA benefits retroactively.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.personal_liability_of_directors: Directors of the IC and of any New Zealand subsidiary may be held personally liable under the companies anti-avoidance rules where the corporate form is a mere facade. The court can pierce the corporate veil under section 15 of the Companies Act 1993, holding directors personally liable for the reconstructed tax debt. Where the directors facilitate a scheme designed to avoid New Zealand tax, they can be charged with being party to tax evasion, incurring imprisonment up to 5 years and a NZD 50,000 fine. A travel ban may be issued while criminal proceeds investigations are pending.

fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.infraction_category: Transfer Pricing Manipulation / Unjustified Service Fees
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.triggering_act: The IC charges its New Zealand branch or related customer a low CUP for fuel supplied from the parent, inflates fuel procurement costs through a related Cook Islands trading entity, pays extraordinary management fees for services never rendered in New Zealand, or finances the New Zealand operation with an artificially high-interest shareholder loan to strip profit.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.statutory_sanction: Inland Revenue may adjust the transaction to the arm's length price under Part 4 of the Income Tax Act 2007, increasing taxable income, disallowing the corresponding interest or expense, and applying a transfer pricing shortfall penalty under section 141AD of up to 150% of the resulting shortfall if a transfer pricing arrangement was not documented contemporaneously and in good faith. A 10% late payment penalty may accrue, and use-of-money interest compounds. If the arrangement has a tax avoidance more than merely incidental purpose, BG 1 applies and penalties escalate. IRD also has power to impose GST adjustments on cross-border related party low-value supplies.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.personal_liability_of_directors: Directors who controlled pricing and knew of the inflated cross-border charges are jointly and severally liable for the corporate tax debt. A director can be personally disqualified by the Financial Markets Authority or Inland Revenue for up to 5 years; in egregious cases of fraudulent transfer pricing, criminal prosecution for obtaining a tax advantage may follow, carrying imprisonment up to 7 years under the Crimes Act 1961 or the Tax Administration Act, alongside a travel ban and asset freezing orders.

fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.infraction_category: Failure to Withhold and Pay NRWT / DTA Abusive Claims
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.triggering_act: The New Zealand payer fails to withhold 15% NRWT from dividends or interest paid to the Cook Islands IC, or fraudulently claims the 5% or 10% reduced DTA rate by presenting a false Cook Islands tax residence certificate without actual tax residence or beneficial ownership.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.statutory_sanction: Under section 144 of the Tax Administration Act 1994, any person who fails to deduct and pay NRWT is liable to pay the full amount of the tax plus an initial penalty of 1% and incremental monthly penalties; in addition, a criminal fine of up to NZD 50,000 and imprisonment for up to 6 months may apply for willful non-payment. A false DTA residence certificate triggers shortfall penalties of up to 150% and for a fraudulent certificate, prosecution under the Crimes Act for forgery with a maximum penalty of 10 years' imprisonment.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.personal_liability_of_directors: The directors of the paying company are personally liable under the PAYE and withholding tax provisions of section 120 of the Tax Administration Act, which imposes directors' civil penalties equal to the unpaid withholding tax plus 100% where the company failed to comply. Directors who personally impressed the false certificate face criminal liability, imprisonment, and a travel ban while subject to the criminal process.

fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.infraction_category: AML / Sanctions Violation for Bunkering Operations
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.triggering_act: The bunkering company supplies fuel to vessels that are flagged in high-risk jurisdictions, owned by individuals on the New Zealand sanctions or anti-money laundering watchlist, or transits from countries subject to UN sanctions, without performing enhanced due diligence; cash payments are accepted for fuel delivery to bypass banking oversight; the IC is used as an opaque conduit to hide the ultimate beneficial owner.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.statutory_sanction: Under the Anti-Money Laundering and Countering Financing of Terrorism Act 2009, an IC carrying on business in New Zealand is a financial institution only if it is a reporting entity; if the bunkering company does not fall under the AML/CFT regime, the breach arises instead through the Crimes Act 1961 handling of proceeds of crime, with a maximum penalty of 7 years' imprisonment for money laundering, and the Proceeds of Crime Act 2015 can confiscate the entire corporate asset base, including vessels and storage tanks. Sanctions violations under the Russia Sanctions Act 2022 or UN Act 1946 can lead to fines up to NZD 1,000,000 and imprisonment up to 14 years.
fatal_compliance_red_flags_and_liabiliti.personal_liability_of_directors: Directors who knew or should have known of the illicit vessel counterparties and failed to terminate the business relationship are personally liable for money laundering facilitation, subject to criminal prosecution, asset freezing, travel bans, and long-term disqualification from holding directorships. The corporate veil is pierced under the Companies Act 1993 where the company was a facade for the laundering activity.
